newsitem.title: USA: Strikes expected to keep GM from reaching goal.
newsitem.headline: Strikes expected to keep GM from reaching goal.

text.p: General Motors Corp. is gaining in the market for cars and small trucks, but strikes this year will prevent it from meeting its goal of a 33 percent U.S. market share, GM Chairman Jack Smith said Thursday.

Smith, speaking to reporters at a breakfast meeting at GM's new global headquarters in Detroit, also said it would be difficult for the automaker to complete the spinoff of 20 percent of its Delphi Automotive Systems parts unit this year.

In addition, he said GM's mid-size car production joint venture in Shanghai, China may not start volume production until April 1999 -- four months late -- because of longer-than-expected negotiatons to obtain final approval from the Chinese government.
Wall Street responded by pushing the world's largest automaker's stock down $1 to $56.75 in consolidated early afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
In 1996, GM had about 31 percent of the U.S. car and truck market. It had hoped the introduction of several new car models would reverse a long-term decline in market share.

"I think we're going to do better than last year, but obviously we're not going to be at the upper limits of what we thought we'd be able to do because of the strikes," Smith said. "It would be tough to hit the 33 percent number with the strikes."

He said a seven-week strike in Oklahoma City has sharply reduced supplies of GM's new Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-sized models, and added that GM cannot make up that lost production this year.
Smith said a tentative agreement to settle the strike in Oklahoma City adds jobs to the plant but still allows the Cutlass and Malibu to remain very competitive cars from a cost standpoint.

"I don't know if I could call it a gain, but we're still in line to have that car be competitive in the marketplace," Smith said, adding that GM "pretty much" maintained the productivity gains associated with the new vehicles.
He said GM will have to spend more money to restart the advertising launch for the Malibu and Cutlass, but added that GM is "not going to go broke on it."
Smith said the recent local strikes were unfortunate but would not deter GM from continuing to improve its manufacturing efficiency.

"I think we've got plants that aren't as competitive as they need to be. We've got a strong push to get those plants competitive," he said. "We believe it is absolutely necessary for the long-term competitiveness of the corporation, and we're striving to get there."
On the Delphi spinoff, Smith said the transaction must follow the sale of GM's Hughes Electronics Corp. defence operations, which is not expected to be completed until the fourth quarter.
"It would be a big challenge to get it done this year," he said of the Delphi spinoff.

Smith and GM Vice Chairman Harry Pearce said the Delphi deal would also have to follow the complete integration of Hughes's Delco Electronics unit into Delphi. That also cannot occur until the sale of Hughes's defence assets to Raytheon Co.
GM announced in January that it would sell the Hughes defence operations to Raytheon in a deal valued at about $9.5 billion.
It is awaiting rulings on tax and antitrust issues related to the Hughes-Raytheon deal and expects those matters to be resolved favourably, Pearce said.

Smith said GM had completed about 70 percent of a $2.5 billion stock buyback programme. He declined to say whether losses from the strikes would affect GM's ability to launch future buyback programmes.
"At the moment, we are continuing to complete the buyback that we started," he said.

Regarding the Shanghai venture, Smith said GM probably does not have enough time to complete construction of the plant to meet the previously scheduled production launch of December 1998, because getting final approval has taken longer than expected.
"Internally, we're saying April of 1999," he said.

GM and Shanghai Automotive Industry Corp. will each own 50 percent of the more than $1 billion joint venture, called Shanghai General Motors Corp. It will eventually have capacity to produce 100,000 Buick-based sedans a year.
